_doc: Closing self-assessment statements per chapter (teacher 2026-11-06: more varied than 'I learned to …'). They replace the chapter's goals at the end of Check your understanding. scripts/inquiry.py sa_goals_html.
fy1-1: I can describe the structure of matter from molecules to quarks.
I can compare sizes with powers of ten and orders of magnitude.
I can recognise the four fundamental interactions in everyday phenomena.
fy1-2: I can convert units with prefixes and powers of ten.
I give a result with a sensible precision.
I can express the same distance in kilometres, astronomical units and light travel time.
fy1-3: I can tell gross, random and systematic errors apart.
I can calculate a mean and estimate the spread of results.
I can judge whether a measurement is repeatable and correct.
fy1-4: I can plot measurements as a graph and fit a line to the points.
I understand what the slope and the intercept tell about the phenomenon.
I notice when a linear model does not fit the data.
fy1-5: I can calculate distance, time or speed in uniform motion.
I can read speed and starting position from a position-time graph.
I can tell distance and position apart.
fy1-6: I can calculate the speed of a freely falling object.
I can read the free-fall acceleration from the slope of a graph.
I understand when mass affects falling and when it does not.
fy1-7: I can calculate mass, volume or density.
I understand what the slope of a mass-volume graph tells.
I can identify a substance from its measured density.
fy1-8: I can formulate a research question and a testable hypothesis.
I can plan a fair experiment.
I can report a result with its uncertainty.
fy2-1: I can recognise the form energy takes in a situation.
I can calculate an unknown energy with the conservation of energy.
I understand why energy is not lost but transformed.
fy2-2: I can follow an energy chain from start to end.
I can express energy with a suitable prefix.
I have a sense of the orders of magnitude of everyday and societal energies.
fy2-3: I can calculate power, energy or time.
I understand why an electricity bill depends on both power and time.
I can calculate electrical energy in kilowatt-hours and its price.
fy2-4: I can calculate the efficiency of a device.
I understand why a real device's efficiency stays below one hundred per cent.
I can read the useful energy and the losses from an energy flow diagram.
fy2-5: I can calculate the energy released by a fuel.
I can compare the energy content of fuels and food.
I can tell released energy and useful energy apart.
fy2-6: I can calculate a power plant's annual energy or average power.
I can classify power plants by weather dependence and controllability.
I can compare forms of production with justified criteria.
fy2-7: I understand how electricity and heat get from a power plant to the user.
I can calculate the energy lost in transmission.
I can justify why electricity is transmitted at a high voltage.
fy2-8: I understand why burning fossil fuels strengthens the greenhouse effect.
I can calculate emissions with an emission factor.
I can justify an energy choice with several criteria.
fy3-1: I understand why force tells the strength of an interaction and how a force meter measures it.
I can tell weight and mass apart, also in everyday speech.
I can calculate an object's weight on Earth and on other celestial bodies.
fy3-2: I can recognise when a force does work and when it does not.
I can calculate work both with the formula and as the area under a graph.
I know what power tells and can compare the power of two devices.
fy3-3: I can describe the state of a gas with its temperature, pressure and volume.
I understand with the particle model what pressure and temperature are.
I can justify why temperatures are compared in kelvins.
fy3-4: I understand how the same force can cause a large or a small pressure.
I can calculate the pressure of a liquid at different depths.
I can read both the constant term and the slope of a pressure-depth graph.
fy3-5: I can tell heat, work and internal energy apart.
I can use the first law of thermodynamics as energy bookkeeping.
I notice when the everyday word 'heat' means something else in physics.
fy3-6: I can calculate the heat that warms a substance.
I understand what specific heat capacity tells about a substance.
I can solve the equilibrium temperature of a calorimeter with energy conservation.
fy3-7: I understand where the energy goes when the temperature stays constant during a change of phase.
I can calculate the heat needed for melting and vaporisation.
I can recognise the stages of a change of phase in a heating curve.
fy3-8: I can explain with the particle model why a solid expands when it warms.
I can plan an experiment to find out what the change in length depends on.
I can calculate the change in an object's length and volume.
fy3-9: I can use Boyle's law in an isothermal process.
I can show with a graph that pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
I understand how the volume of a gas depends on its kelvin temperature.
fy3-10: I can infer from pressure, volume and temperature how much gas there is.
I can use the ideal gas law.
I understand gas pressure as particles colliding with the walls.
fy3-11: I can calculate the work of an expanding gas and see it as the area under a graph.
I understand why a heat engine cannot turn all heat into work.
I can calculate the efficiency of a heat engine.
fy3-12: I can recognise conduction, convection and thermal radiation in everyday situations.
I can calculate the heat flow through a wall or a window.
I can explain the greenhouse effect with the energy balance.
fy3-13: I can turn measurement data into a straight line and extend it.
I can determine absolute zero from my own measurements.
I can estimate the uncertainty of a result with the steepest and the shallowest line.
fy3-14: I understand why ice cools a drink so effectively.
I can decide by comparing amounts of heat whether all the ice melts.
I can calculate the equilibrium temperature when part of a substance melts.
fy3-15: I can calculate the efficiency of a power plant chain from the efficiencies of its stages.
I know where the largest energy loss of a condensing power plant occurs.
I understand why combined heat and power makes better use of the fuel.
fy3-16: I can combine several heat phenomena into one energy balance.
I can justify whether energy goes into warming or into a change of phase.
I dare to take on a multi-step everyday heat problem.
fy4-1: I can describe motion as position as a function of time.
I can calculate displacement and velocity with their signs.
I read the velocity of uniform motion from the slope of a graph.
fy4-2: I understand what the sign of acceleration tells.
I can calculate velocity, position and time in uniformly accelerated motion.
I can determine the free-fall acceleration from measurements.
fy4-3: I understand why motion continues without a force pushing it forward.
I can recognise a force and its reaction pair.
I can calculate an unknown force when the net force is zero.
fy4-4: I understand how acceleration depends on the net force and the mass.
I can infer the direction of the net force, also in slowing motion.
I can use Newton's second law in calculations.
fy4-5: I can recognise the forces on an object and draw a force diagram.
I can split a force into components.
I can write the equations of motion from a force diagram.
fy4-6: I can tell static and kinetic friction apart.
I can draw the force diagram of an object on a slope.
I can determine a coefficient of friction experimentally.
fy4-7: I can calculate kinetic and potential energy relative to a chosen zero level.
I understand why kinetic energy grows with the square of speed.
fy4-8: I understand when mechanical energy is conserved and where it goes.
I can calculate speed or height with energy conservation.
I can calculate the work of friction or another force with the work-energy principle.
fy4-9: I can calculate momentum and its change with signs.
I can read impulse as the area under a force-time graph.
I understand why a longer stopping time reduces the force.
fy4-10: I understand why total momentum is conserved in a collision.
I can calculate velocities in collisions and explosions.
I can tell elastic and inelastic collisions apart.
fy4-11: I can calculate a stopping distance and its parts.
I can judge how speed, reaction time and road conditions affect stopping.
I understand why seat belts and airbags protect.
fy4-12: I can calculate when and where two objects meet.
I can read a meeting from the intersection of graphs.
I understand how the velocities affect the meeting.
fy4-13: I can draw a separate force diagram for each connected object.
I can calculate the acceleration and tension of connected objects.
I understand why the tension is not the weight of the hanging object.
fy4-14: I understand why a falling object reaches terminal velocity.
I can draw a force diagram that includes air resistance.
I can calculate acceleration when air resistance is not neglected.
fy4-15: I understand how hydro and wind power plants produce electricity.
I can calculate a power plant's power, efficiency and energy.
I can justify why wind power depends so strongly on wind speed.
fy4-16: I can choose whether to solve a situation with equations of motion or the energy principle.
I can calculate the normal force in an accelerating lift.
I dare to take on a multi-step mechanics problem.
fy5-1: I understand what torque and the lever arm are.
I can calculate torque also for a force at an angle.
I can calculate the net torque using signs.
fy5-2: I can write the equilibrium conditions of an object.
I can calculate support forces with the torque condition.
I understand how the centre of mass decides whether an object tips over.
fy5-3: I understand why velocity changes in circular motion although speed stays the same.
I can infer where an object goes when the force keeping it on the circle stops.
fy5-4: I can recognise the direction of centripetal acceleration.
I can apply Newton's second law to circular motion.
I understand which force turns a car in a bend.
fy5-5: I understand that two objects pull each other with equal forces.
I can calculate the gravitational force and field strength.
I can explain how gravity gathers matter into stars and galaxies.
fy5-6: I understand why a satellite stays in orbit and an astronaut is weightless.
I can calculate a satellite's orbital speed and period.
I can judge when a circular orbit model is good.
fy5-7: I can read the amplitude, period and frequency of an oscillation from a graph.
I can calculate displacement with a sine model.
I can fit a sine function to measurements and interpret the result.
fy5-8: I can recognise a harmonic force and its direction.
I can determine a spring constant from the slope of a graph.
I can calculate the potential energy of a spring.
fy5-9: I know which quantities affect the period of an oscillation.
I can calculate the period of a spring and a pendulum.
I can measure a period and estimate its uncertainty.
fy5-10: I understand what a wave carries with it.
I can tell transverse and longitudinal waves apart.
I can use the basic wave equation.
fy5-11: I can apply the law of reflection.
I know how a pulse reflects from a fixed and a free end of a rope.
I can explain diffraction with Huygens' principle.
fy5-12: I understand what happens when two waves meet.
I can infer from the path difference whether interference is constructive or destructive.
I know what the Fourier transform is used for in sound analysis.
fy5-13: I can recognise the nodes and antinodes of a standing wave.
I can calculate the natural frequencies of a string and a pipe.
I can compare the sounds of open and closed pipes.
fy5-14: I understand what determines pitch and timbre.
I can read the fundamental and overtones from an FFT graph.
I can explain the Doppler effect and calculate the heard frequency.
fy5-15: I can calculate a sound level in decibels.
I understand why two equally loud sources do not double the decibels.
fy5-16: I can assess the harm of noise and calculate the reference time of a noise dose.
I can compare ways of reducing noise.
I understand the working principle of a loudspeaker and a microphone.
fy5-17: I can calculate the depth of a boundary from an echo time.
I understand how ultrasound frequency affects image resolution.
I can determine the distance of an earthquake from the arrival times of its waves.
fy6-1: I understand why electric current is not used up in a lamp.
I can calculate current, charge and transferred energy.
I can draw and read a circuit diagram.
fy6-2: I can connect an ammeter and a voltmeter correctly and justify why.
I can choose a measuring range and estimate the error limit of a reading.
I understand how a wrong connection changes the circuit.
fy6-3: I can determine the resistance of a component.
I can interpret a characteristic curve.
I understand how a wire's dimensions affect its resistance.
fy6-4: I understand how current and voltage divide in series and parallel circuits.
I can calculate a total resistance.
I can solve a mixed circuit step by step.
fy6-5: I can use Kirchhoff's current law.
I can read a potential diagram.
I understand why the source voltage divides over the resistors of a loop.
fy6-6: I can calculate the power of a component and the energy transformed in it.
I can compare how power divides in series and parallel circuits.
I understand why a resistor's temperature levels off.
fy6-7: I can calculate the electrical energy a device uses.
I can calculate an electricity bill from meter readings.
I understand why consumption depends on energy, not power.
fy6-8: I understand why a battery's terminal voltage drops as the current grows.
I can determine the source voltage and internal resistance from a graph.
I know why a short circuit is dangerous.
fy6-9: I can calculate a battery's charge and energy.
I can calculate the charging current in a charging circuit.
I understand why the charging current decreases as the battery fills.
fy6-10: I understand charging and induction as charge moving.
I can calculate the force between point charges with Coulomb's law.
I can describe an electric field with field lines.
fy6-11: I can calculate electric field strength.
I understand why the field between plates is uniform.
I can determine the force on a charged particle.
fy6-12: I can calculate the work done by an electric field with potentials.
I understand why positive and negative charges move in opposite directions in a field.
I can calculate the kinetic energy of an accelerated particle in electronvolts.
fy6-13: I can calculate a capacitor's charge and capacitance.
I understand how a dielectric changes a capacitor.
I can describe the charging and discharging of a capacitor.
fy6-14: I understand a diode's forward and reverse direction.
I can size the series resistor of an LED.
I can interpret a solar cell graph and calculate its efficiency.
fy6-15: I can infer whether a fuse's rated current is exceeded.
I can judge how dangerous a current through the body is.
I know how earthing and a residual current device protect.
fy6-16: I can calculate the charging time and cost of an electric car.
I can compare single-phase and three-phase charging.
I understand why a loose connection heats up.
fy7-1: I understand why a magnet attracts iron and turns a compass.
I can draw and interpret magnetic field lines.
I can calculate the sum of two perpendicular fields.
fy7-2: I understand why the magnetic force bends a particle's path but does not change its speed.
I can determine the direction and size of the magnetic force.
I can calculate a particle's mass in a mass spectrometer.
fy7-3: I can infer the field direction of a wire and a coil with the right-hand rule.
I can calculate the magnetic flux density of a straight wire and a coil.
I can determine a constant from measurements with a fitted line.
fy7-4: I can calculate the magnetic force on a current-carrying wire.
I understand why parallel currents attract or repel each other.
I can explain how a DC motor and a loudspeaker work.
fy7-5: I can calculate magnetic flux and induced voltage.
I can infer the induced voltage from the slope of a flux graph.
I understand why a voltage appears in a moving rod.
fy7-6: I can infer the direction of an induced current with Lenz's law.
I understand why the induced current opposes the change.
I can recognise applications of eddy currents in everyday life.
fy7-7: I understand why a rotating coil produces an alternating voltage.
I can calculate the peak voltage of a generator.
I can calculate rms values and average power.
fy7-8: I understand why a transformer does not work with direct current.
I can calculate a transformer's voltages, currents and numbers of turns.
I can justify why electricity is transmitted at high voltage.
fy7-9: I understand how electromagnetic radiation is produced.
I can use the relation between wavelength and frequency.
I can infer an object's temperature from the colour of its glow.
fy7-10: I understand why light refracts at a boundary.
I can calculate angles of refraction and the speed of light in a material.
I can determine a refractive index from measurements.
fy7-11: I understand why a prism splits white light.
I can calculate the refraction angles of different colours.
I can explain how a rainbow forms.
fy7-12: I know when light is totally internally reflected.
I can calculate the critical angle.
I understand how an optical fibre guides light.
fy7-13: I understand how interference and diffraction arise in a grating.
I can use the grating equation.
I can determine a laser's wavelength from measurements.
fy7-14: I understand why reflections from a thin film reinforce or cancel each other.
I can calculate a film thickness from the interference conditions.
I can explain the colours of a soap bubble.
fy7-15: I understand why polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave.
I can predict how polarisers change the light passing through.
I know why polarised glasses reduce glare.
fy7-16: I understand how a wireless charger and an induction hob use induction.
I can judge why wireless charging weakens with distance.
I can calculate fibre attenuation in decibels.
fy8-1: I understand why the photoelectric effect needs the photon model.
I can calculate a photon's energy in joules and electronvolts.
I can use the photoelectric equation.
fy8-2: I understand why a gas spectrum has lines.
I can calculate a line's wavelength from the energy difference of states.
I can identify an element from its spectrum.
fy8-3: I can calculate the energy of a photon from a transition in hydrogen.
I understand why hydrogen emits only certain wavelengths.
I can assess the strengths and weaknesses of the Bohr model.
fy8-4: I understand how the double-slit pattern builds up from single hits.
I can explain the Compton effect with photon momentum.
I can calculate a photon's momentum.
fy8-5: I understand how standing waves lead to the allowed states of an electron.
I can interpret an orbital picture correctly.
I can calculate the number of orbitals and electrons in a shell.
fy8-6: I understand why an LED's threshold voltage depends on its colour.
I can determine a threshold voltage from a graph.
I can determine Planck's constant from my own measurements.
fy8-7: I understand the role of stimulated emission and population inversion in a laser.
I can calculate a laser's wavelength and the number of photons.
I know how a quantum dot's size determines its colour.
fy8-8: I understand how the atomic number and mass number change in each decay.
I can infer nuclear energy levels from a gamma spectrum.
fy8-9: I understand why random decay gives a constant half-life.
I can calculate the number of nuclei and the activity.
I can determine a half-life from measurement data.
fy8-10: I can calculate the mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus.
I understand why both fusion and fission can release energy.
I can calculate the energy of a nuclear reaction.
fy8-11: I understand the energy of fission and fusion through binding energy.
I can calculate the energy of a nuclear reaction from atomic masses.
I can assess claims about nuclear power with physics.
fy8-12: I can compare the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
I can calculate the attenuation of gamma radiation.
I understand how ionising radiation damages cells.
fy8-13: I can calculate a radiation dose with weighting factors.
I know where a Finn's radiation dose mainly comes from.
I can judge how time, distance and shielding reduce the dose.
fy8-14: I understand how contrast arises in an X-ray image.
I know how a PET scanner locates a tracer.
I can justify the safety solutions of radiotherapy.
fy8-15: I can infer from conservation laws whether a particle reaction is possible.
I understand beta decay at the quark level.
fy8-16: I can calculate a galaxy's distance with the Hubble–Lemaître law.
I understand what the background radiation tells about the early universe.
I know in which stages the elements were formed.
fy9-koe: I know the structure of the matriculation exam and how many tasks I choose from each part.
I can write a solution that shows the reasoning, the units and a check that the answer makes sense.
I can use the diagnostic test to pick the chapters I review first.
fy9-mittaaminen: I can draw a graph from measurement data and choose a suitable fit.
I understand what the slope and the intercept of a graph tell about the phenomenon.
I can state a result to a justified precision and estimate its uncertainty.
fy9-kokeellisuus: I can plan an experiment in which only the studied quantity changes.
I recognise a systematic error in a graph and tell it apart from random scatter.
I can assess the shortcomings of a lab report and write a justified conclusion.
fy9-energia: I can solve energy, power and efficiency problems with the units substituted.
I can interpret energy flow diagrams and graphs of consumption data.
I can tell a justified claim about energy production from an unjustified one.
fy9-lampo: I can set up a heat balance equation that includes a change of state.
I can read from a heating curve where the substance warms up and where its state changes.
I recognise the main sources of error in a heat experiment and their direction.
fy9-kaasut: I remember to use the kelvin temperature and the total pressure in gas problems.
I can interpret a graph of gas measurements and its extrapolation.
I can assess when the ideal gas model describes a situation well enough.
fy9-liike: I can choose whether a problem needs the model of uniform or of uniformly accelerated motion.
I can find the acceleration and the distance travelled from a $(t,v)$ graph.
I can tell the motions of two objects apart in the same graph.
fy9-voimat: I can draw a force diagram of a new situation without a model.
I can write the equation of motion for friction, slope and connected-body situations.
I recognise a wrong force diagram and can explain what is wrong in it.
fy9-sailymislait: I can choose whether to solve a problem with conservation of energy or of momentum.
I can interpret graphs of braking and collision data.
I understand why momentum is conserved in a collision even when kinetic energy is not.
fy9-ympyraliike: I can solve an equilibrium problem with torques.
I understand which force acts as the centripetal force in different circular motions.
I can explain why weightlessness is felt in a satellite.
fy9-aallot: I can choose a suitable model for an oscillation, wave or sound problem.
I can read the period, wavelength and amplitude from oscillation and wave graphs.
I can tell the loudness and the pitch of a sound apart in measurements.
fy9-tasavirta: I can solve the currents and voltages of a circuit with Kirchhoff's laws.
I can find the emf and internal resistance of a battery from a graph.
I can assess claims about electrical energy and batteries by calculating.
fy9-sahkokentta: I can tell electric field strength, potential and voltage apart.
I can find the capacitance from the slope of a graph of measurements.
I can justify electrical safety instructions with physics.
fy9-magnetismi-valo: I can choose a suitable model for a magnetism, induction or light problem and check its conditions.
I can interpret graphs of magnetic field and light measurements.
I understand why electricity is transmitted over long distances at a high voltage.
fy9-moderni: I can choose a suitable model for a photon, atom or nucleus problem.
I can find the work function and the Planck constant from a graph of the photoelectric effect.
I can assess claims about radiation and nuclear energy with justification.
